description: A solder bridge joins U1's two supply pins. U1 is an ATMEGA328P-PU in a DIP-28: 2.54 mm pin pitch, 1.3 mm pads, so the copper edges of pins 7 (VCC_5V) and 8 (GND) stand 1.24 mm apart. A fillet on pin 7 stands proud of the pad, wets onto pin 8's shoulder, and ties the ATmega's supply to its ground. The rail collapses to a few tens of millivolts, the part does not reset — it does not start — and the board is dead in a way that looks like a dead chip. The relay, the DHT22 and the LED are all fine; a technician who does not suspect a short will replace the MCU and the sensor before looking at the solder.
seed_target: The COPPER of board_base.json, never the netlist. One extra netless track is added: a 1.3 mm-wide F.Cu track from the centre of U1's pad 7 at (16.51, 21.59) to the centre of U1's pad 8 at (16.51, 24.13), with no net assigned to it, because no net was ever assigned to it. A solder bridge is EXTRA metal, not a reroute, and the netless form is what a bridge actually is: a bridge carrying one of the two nets would say — wrongly — that the designer had routed VCC_5V onto the ground pad. The site was chosen by the rule in mutate.py, and the rule is a contact argument, not a coordinate lookup: (1) both pads on the same layer, so a lump of solder can physically reach both; (2) different nets, so the bridge is a short and not a piece of metal doing nothing; (3) the same component, because a bridge inside one part is the ordinary way a short happens and the case a reader of the board can recognise; (4) the pad-to-pad gap no wider than FILLET_SPAN_MAX (1.3 mm), the widest gap a solder fillet is taken to bridge, so the defect is a plausible assembly fault and not a wire someone laid across the board; (5) the drawn bridge touches copper of EXACTLY those two nets and nothing else — no third net, no netless pad — so the short it makes is the one the reader is meant to find. Among the sites that pass all five, the seed prefers a supply-to-supply pair (a bridge that ties the rail to ground destroys the board, a bridge between two signal nets makes one function misbehave) and then takes the closest pair, ties broken by (ref, pin_a, pin_b) so the choice is a total order. The result is 40 tracks in the base and 41 in the defective board — one netless track added, and nothing else changed.
notes: The defect is in the copper, so the netlist is untouched: U1 pin 7 is still VCC_5V and U1 pin 8 is still GND, and board_defective.json is judged against the same netlist as board_base.json — the product's own path, where compile_board calls verify_board(board, netlist) with the netlist it just compiled from. Nothing else in the tree can see it, and each reason is structural rather than a missing rule: III.1 asks whether each required connection is made (it is — both nets are still routed), III.1c and III.1d ask whether the ground pour still reaches the ground pads (it does), III.3 and III.4 ask whether the pin-to-net map matches the netlist (it does), IV.1 asks whether the land patterns match a table (they do), and IV.2 compares pinouts against KiCad symbols (it cannot even run for these parts). III.2 is the only check that asks the question a bridge raises: union-find over every copper object on the board, net-agnostic, then a count of the distinct nets each group carries. A group carrying more than one net is a short. Measured: board_base.json passes III.2; board_defective.json fails it with 'nets [GND, VCC_5V] joined'; and no other check changes.
